One example is the revolt of Abū Ḥarb al-Mubarqaʿ al-Yamānī during the caliphate of al-Muʿtaṣim ibn al-Rashīd. Abū Ḥarb appeared in the mountains of Jordan and declared rebellion against the state, wearing a veil over his face during the day to conceal his identity. Many peasants in the region joined him. The state was unable to crush his movement until the planting season, when his peasant followers became occupied with working the land. Other examples include the revolt of the Alid al-Ḥasan ibn Zayd and his establishment of an Alid state in Ṭabaristān; the rise of the Ṣaffārid state in Ṭabaristān, 254–290 AH; and Aḥmad ibn Ṭūlūn’s establishment of an independent state in Egypt. See ʿUlyān, Qarāmiṭat al-ʿIrāq, pp. 125, 127.↩︎

When the Abbasid caliph al-Muʿtazz ibn al-Mutawakkil (252–255 AH/866–868 CE) could no longer tolerate the pressure placed on him by the Turkish troops and their demands, he tried to counter them by calling on the Maghribi troops—that is, the Arab soldiers in the Abbasid army. But al-Muʿtazz was unable to pay the soldiers’ wages, so the Turkish and Arab troops ended up united against the caliph himself and together took part in killing him. See Ibn al-Wardī, Tārīkh, p. 332. In other words, the Arab soldiers’ hostility toward the politically dominant Turks did not prevent them from joining their “class comrades,” the Turkish soldiers, when their shared material interests brought them together—even though the caliph they killed was himself an Arab.↩︎

One of the many ways ordinary people engaged in social struggle at the time can be seen in the following incident. After the killing of al-Muʿtazz ibn al-Mutawakkil, the Turks installed Muḥammad ibn al-Wāthiq as caliph and gave him the title al-Muhtadī (255–256 AH/868–869 CE). But al-Muhtadī disappointed them. He tried to reduce extravagance, improve the machinery of government, and improve the condition of those suffering injustice. This angered the Turks who had put him in power, and they began plotting to remove him or kill him, as they had done before. The “common people” sensed the beginnings of the plot and took a stand in defense of the caliph. They prepared leaflets and scattered them in the streets and mosques. The leaflets read: “Muslims! Pray to God for your just caliph, that God may give him victory over his enemy, protect him from his oppressor, and complete His blessing upon him and upon this community by preserving his life. The Turks have forced him to abdicate.” See al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Umam, vol. 7, pp. 571–572.↩︎
The Sawād of Kufa means its villages and countryside.↩︎

“The sciences of the ancients” was a term used by medieval Arab scholars, philosophers, and historians of philosophy for the ancient natural and philosophical sciences that were translated into Arabic and then became part of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage. The term refers above all to the sciences of ancient Greece, but also to Persian, Indian, and other ancient sources that contributed to Arab culture in the Abbasid period. We prefer this older term to the modern expression “foreign sciences” when speaking of medieval Arab culture. “The sciences of the ancients” reflects a scientific view of civilization as a historical succession shared among peoples, nations, and regions, without restricting it to one people or one geographical area. “Foreign sciences,” by contrast, implies an opposite and unscientific view of civilization. No science is “foreign” in relation to any people on earth.↩︎

The Sufis claim that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī was the first Sufi and the pioneer of Sufism. In reality, neither his conduct nor his thought went beyond the asceticism of his own time in either character or content. Indeed, in practice he may be counted among the more moderate ascetics, since he did not go to extremes in seclusion or worship. He is famous for saying: “An atom’s weight of sound piety is better than a thousand weights of fasting and prayer” (al-Risāla al-Qushayriyya, p. 54). Despite the simplicity and conventional Islamic meaning of this statement, later Sufis treated it as evidence that al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī was one of them, or even their pioneer. Yet ordinary Muslim believers say the same thing, as do the leading scholars of Sunni Islam and the jurists, especially—even when they are hostile to Sufism.↩︎

al-Ṭūsī says of the Sufis in al-Lumaʿ, p. 42: “They were named after the outward appearance of their clothing, not after any branch of knowledge or spiritual state by which they were known, because wearing wool was the practice of the prophets, peace be upon them, of the truthful, and the mark of poor worshippers.” In al-Kalābādhī’s al-Taʿarruf li-Madhhab al-Taṣawwuf (d. 380 AH/990 CE), Cairo ed., 1923, ch. 1, he says of the Sufis: “They were called Sufis because of their clothing and appearance. They did not wear, for the pleasure of the self, clothes that were soft to the touch or beautiful to look at. They dressed only to cover themselves, and so deliberately chose rough haircloth and coarse wool.” al-Kalābādhī also reports al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī as saying: “I met seventy men who had fought at Badr, and they wore nothing but wool.”↩︎

The picture al-Masʿūdī gives us of social conditions at the end of the Umayyad period may help show what we mean by the development of social and political conflict. He reports that after the fall of the Umayyad state, one of its elders was asked why it had collapsed. He answered: “We became so occupied with our pleasures that we neglected what we were obliged to watch over. We wronged our subjects, so they lost hope of justice from us. Our officials mistreated them, so they longed to be rid of us. We burdened the taxpayers, so they abandoned us. Our estates were ruined, and with them our treasuries. We trusted our ministers, and they put their own interests before ours. They carried out affairs without us and hid knowledge of them from us. The pay of our soldiers was delayed, so they stopped obeying us. Our enemy called them over, and they joined him in fighting us. Our enemies came after us, and we were unable to resist because we had so few supporters...” The words may not really have been spoken by an Umayyad, but the picture they paint accurately reflects the historical reality of the final days of the Umayyad state. See al-Masʿūdī, Murūj al-Dhahab, vol. 2, p. 194.↩︎

The ideological side of this practice lies in its preparing the way for what the Sufis later called walāya, or sainthood. The Sufis created this rank for those among them who reached the highest spiritual stations, and attributed to their “saints” divine wonders similar to the miracles of prophets. The real basis of this Sufi idea of sainthood was an attempt to take absolute religious authority away from the caliphs, whose monopoly on the title “God’s caliph and His shadow on earth” formed part of the official religious ideology of the caliphate. The creation of Sufi sainthood was therefore one of many different ways in which the ideology of the state was challenged.↩︎
